# qang as a module: changes to quantum and machine-learning libraries {#sec-ch35}

Every chapter of this book noted what it would ask of an existing library. This chapter delivers that list. qang 0.13.0
ships a new subpackage, `qang.integrations`, with one module per library: mitiq, qiskit-experiments, Qiskit Dynamics, QuTiP,
Stim, scikit-learn, JAX, PyTorch, Qibo, pytket, Amazon Braket and NVIDIA's CUDA-Q. Each module brings qang's three things
(the readings, the filter and the closed-form rules) into that library's own terms and has its test in
`tests/test_integrations.py`. The figures in this chapter come from `tools/make_cap35_numbers.py`, which runs in three
environments because not every library fits in one. None comes from real hardware. The chapter separates what is done and
tested inside qang from what would still have to be proposed to each project.

## From the base: what each library gets {#sec-base35}

The Chapter 1 base is a probability $p_0$ and its readings, $qg_Z=2p_0-1$, $m=1000\,qg_Z$ and $\theta=\arccos qg_Z$. What
qang adds to another library is always one of three things:

- **a reading**: turn what the library already measures (counts, populations, detectors, probabilities) into $qg_Z$ and m-qg,
  with a single qubit order (Chapter 32);
- **the filter**: keep the shots in the circuit's Hamming-weight sector, with the kept fraction $K$ (Chapters 21 and 22);
- **a closed-form rule**: the filter's cost rule (Chapter 21), the closed form of heralded calibration (§31) or the minimal
  pulse area (§160).

## How it is built {#sec-design35}

- **Nothing extra gets imported.** `import qang` still needs only NumPy. Each submodule imports its library when asked, and if
  the library is missing, the error says what to install: `pip install "qang[mitiq]"`, `qang[stim]`, and so on.
- **One extra per library** in `pyproject.toml`, plus one, `integrations`, with every library that can share an environment.
- **Each test skips itself** if its library is not installed. That is why the repository's CI, which installs `qang[all]`,
  runs the scikit-learn tests and skips the rest.

## Mitigation: mitiq {#sec-mitiq35}

mitiq can already post-select on Hamming weight: its `post_select` ships with that very example. There was no need to write it
again. What qang adds on top is:

- `qg_z` and `filtered_qg_z`, to read a `MeasurementResult` in qg;
- `qg_executor`, which turns a sampler into the real-valued executor that mitiq's techniques use;
- `execute_with_filter_zne`, which combines the filter with zero-noise extrapolation;
- `filter_rule`, the Chapter 21 rule.

The script runs a three-qubit weight-1 circuit (Givens rotations in Cirq), with amplitude damping of 0.05 and dephasing of
0.03 per moment, and reads qubit 1. The exact value is $-257.3$ m-qg:

| noise | raw | filtered | raw + ZNE | filtered + ZNE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | 233.2 | **0.0** | 49.4 | **0.0** |
| T1 + dephasing | 257.9 | 30.3 | 55.9 | **1.1** |

: Error in m-qg of the qubit-1 reading, Richardson ZNE with factors 1, 3 and 5 and global folding. {#tbl-mitiq35}

With T1 alone the filter is exact (Chapter 21, F1) and ZNE has nothing to correct. With T1 and dephasing, the filter leaves
only the dephasing and ZNE removes it (F6): the error drops from 30.3 to 1.1 m-qg. ZNE on the raw reading stays at 55.9 m-qg,
because T1 does not scale well under folding. **The proposal for mitiq** is the combination: post-selection, then ZNE, with
the cost rule deciding whether to filter. The separate pieces already existed.

## Calibration: qiskit-experiments {#sec-experiments35}

`HeraldedReadout` is an experiment in the framework with two circuits (herald, I or X, measure) and an analysis with the §31
closed form. It runs on the Aer simulator with readout error $e_{01}=0.015$, $e_{10}=0.04$, and with a thermal population $p$
prepared by purification:

| $p$ | $e_{01}$ standard | $e_{01}$ qg | $e_{10}$ standard | $e_{10}$ qg | $p$ qg | $T_{\text{eff}}$ (5 GHz) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.0148 | 0.0151 | 0.0401 | 0.0396 | 0.0000 | 0 mK |
| 0.01 | 0.0244 | 0.0151 | 0.0494 | 0.0397 | 0.0099 | 52.1 mK |
| 0.03 | 0.0431 | 0.0151 | 0.0683 | 0.0396 | 0.0297 | 68.8 mK |
| 0.08 | 0.0900 | 0.0150 | 0.1152 | 0.0401 | 0.0794 | 97.9 mK |

: Standard calibration against heralded calibration, 200,000 shots per circuit. {#tbl-experiments35}

The standard calibration adds the temperature to the readout error, $e_{01}+p\,b$, and sees the qubit as cold. The closed form
separates the two. This is the result of §31 and Chapter 27, now inside a `BaseExperiment` run with `exp.run(backend)`. **It is
the most concrete proposal in this chapter** for qiskit-experiments, because Chapter 18 showed that the standard calibration
can leave a random-number certifier unsafe.

## Open systems: QuTiP {#sec-qutip35}

`qg_readings` reads $(qg_X,qg_Y,qg_Z)$ of each qubit of a `Qobj`, `mesolve_qg` reads a `mesolve` evolution, and `t1_collapse`
builds the collapse operators for equal T1. With a three-qubit W state and $t/T_1=0.6$, the raw reading of each qubit is
$+634.1$ m-qg and the filtered one is $+333.333$, the noiseless value. The kept fraction is $0.5488=e^{-0.6}$, as Chapter 21
predicts. It is the same check Chapters 19 and 21 made by integrating Lindblad by hand, now with QuTiP's integrator.

## Error correction: Stim {#sec-stim35}

A detector that fires with probability $p$ reads $qg=1-2p$. With the distance-5 repetition code, 5 rounds and 200,000 samples:

| noise $p$ | detectors (m-qg) | raw logical | decoded logical |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.01 | 972.4 to 1000.0 | 933.7 | 1000.0 |
| 0.03 | 919.0 to 1000.0 | 815.2 | 999.1 |
| 0.06 | 841.8 to 1000.0 | 660.1 | 993.7 |

: qg readings of a repetition code in Stim; decoding with PyMatching. {#tbl-stim35}

Decoding is bringing the logical qubit to the pole. The last-round detectors sit at $+1000$ because the noise enters before each
round. `measurement_qg` also applies the filter to the measurement records. **The proposal for Stim/PyMatching** is still the
one from Chapter 26, the T1-aware reweighting (2.1 to 2.5 times), which this module does not implement yet.

## Learning: scikit-learn, JAX and PyTorch {#sec-ml35}

- **scikit-learn.** `WeightQNNClassifier` and `MultiClassQNNClassifier` have `fit`, `predict`, `decision_function` and `score`,
  accept any labels and work in `Pipeline`, `cross_val_score` and `GridSearchCV`. On the two-moons set (120 points), with T1 of
  0.15 and 5-fold cross-validation, the filtered model scores 0.833 ± 0.083 and the raw one 0.842 ± 0.081. **There is no
  difference**, as in Chapter 20: trained under the calibrated noise, the model without the filter catches up. `GridSearchCV`
  can choose `qang=True/False` like any other hyperparameter.
- **JAX.** The readings and the filter written with `jax.numpy` go through `jit`, `grad` and `vmap`. The gradient of a filtered
  loss through a PennyLane QNode with `interface="jax"` matches finite differences to $2\cdot10^{-10}$. That was what
  Chapter 20 left untested. Getting there turned up a conflict: PennyLane 0.45 uses `jax.core.is_concrete`, which JAX 0.12
  removed, and it works only with JAX < 0.9.
- **PyTorch.** `WeightQNNTorch` is an `nn.Module`: a PennyLane `TorchLayer` with `SingleExcitation` rotations, which conserve
  the weight, the filtered reading and a linear layer. With T1 of 0.1 per layer, the filtered reading differs from the clean
  one by $1.2\cdot10^{-16}$ and the raw one by 262.5 m-qg. The gradient flows through `backward()`.

## Pulses: Qiskit Dynamics {#sec-dynamics35}

`rabi_qg` solves a resonantly driven qubit and returns $qg_Z$. Against $\cos A$, with $A$ the pulse area, the error is
$1.1\cdot10^{-7}$ to $5\cdot10^{-7}$ with a square pulse and $5\cdot10^{-7}$ to $1.9\cdot10^{-6}$ with a Gaussian pulse, for
$A$ equal to $\pi/2$, $\pi$ and 2.2. It is the basis of the §160 minimal-area rule. **The conflict**: Qiskit Dynamics 0.6
requires `qiskit<=1.3`, so it does not coexist with Qiskit 2.x and needs its own environment.

## SDKs: Qibo, pytket, Braket and CUDA-Q {#sec-sdks35}

Each gets the qang rotation ($R_Y(\arccos qg)$) and the canonical reading with the filter:

- **Qibo**: the reading of $qg=0.6$ with 100,000 shots gives 0.5978;
- **pytket**: gives the exact value, $-0.25$, from the statevector. pytket measures angles in half-turns, not radians, and
  `rqang` does the conversion. It is the kind of unit error this scale is meant to prevent;
- **Braket**: runs on the `LocalSimulator`, so it is no longer just a result format (Chapter 32); the reading of 0.2 gives
  0.201;
- **CUDA-Q**: runs in WSL with CUDA-Q 0.16.0. On the CPU simulator (`qpp-cpu`), the reading of $-0.5$ gives $-0.5018$ and
  the filter keeps 0.7509, against 0.75 expected. The GPU simulator (`nvidia`, cuStateVec) did not start, because the CUDA
  driver WSL sees is older than CUDA-Q's runtime. The Windows NVIDIA driver needs updating; the code does not change, only
  `cudaq.set_target("nvidia")`.

## What to propose to each project {#sec-proposals35}

What is in `qang.integrations` already works. What follows is what would be worth taking to each project, ordered by the
backing it has in the book:

| project | proposal | backing | strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| qiskit-experiments | heralded calibration: separates temperature and readout | §31, Chapters 18 and 27, @tbl-experiments35 | **strong** |
| mitiq | post-selection + ZNE with the cost rule | Chapter 21, @tbl-mitiq35 | **strong** |
| scikit-learn (via qang) | weight QNN as an estimator | Chapter 20 | useful, no accuracy gain |
| PennyLane | fix compatibility with JAX ≥ 0.9 (`is_concrete`) | this chapter | a real ecosystem bug |
| Qiskit Dynamics | Qiskit 2.x support | this chapter | a real ecosystem bug |
| PyMatching / Stim | T1-aware reweighting | Chapter 26 | moderate (loses 15 % under depolarizing noise) |
| Qiskit transpiler | keep N-conserving gates | Chapter 24 | moderate |
| qiskit-machine-learning | filter as a Gram-matrix repair | Chapter 23 | weak (a single kernel) |

: Proposals for each project, with their backing. {#tbl-proposals35}

## Environment conflicts {#sec-conflicts35}

Putting everything in one environment was not possible, and the conflicts are information:

- Qiskit Dynamics 0.6 requires `qiskit<=1.3`;
- PennyLane 0.45 does not work with JAX ≥ 0.9;
- amazon-braket-sdk pins `cloudpickle==2.2.1`, while recent joblib (used by scikit-learn) needs ≥ 3.0. Both worked with
  cloudpickle 3.1.2, but pip warns about the conflict;
- mitiq 1.1 pulled NumPy down to 2.2.6;
- CUDA-Q has no wheels for Windows and was tested in WSL; its GPU simulator needs a newer NVIDIA driver.

That is why there are three environments: `.venv-int` with almost everything, `.venv-dyn` for Qiskit Dynamics and WSL for
CUDA-Q. The book's `.venv` was left untouched.

## Without qang and with qang {#sec-comparison35}

| library | without qang | with qang | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| mitiq | `post_select` and ZNE separately | ZNE of the filtered reading + rule | 55.9 → 1.1 m-qg under T1 and dephasing |
| qiskit-experiments | $e_{01}$ inflated by $p\,b$, "cold" qubit | unbiased $e_{01}$, $p$ and $T_{\text{eff}}$ | separates two errors the standard mixes up |
| QuTiP | operator expectations | readings in m-qg and the filter | filter exact under T1 to $10^{-6}$ |
| Stim | detection rates | detectors and logicals in m-qg | unit only |
| scikit-learn | no estimator for the QNN | `fit`/`predict`, CV, search | API; same accuracy (0.833 against 0.842) |
| JAX | filtered reading untested | `jit`/`grad`, $2\cdot10^{-10}$ | tested, with JAX < 0.9 |
| PyTorch | no weight layer | `WeightQNNTorch` | filter exact under T1 inside torch |
| Dynamics | populations | $qg_Z=\cos A$ to $10^{-6}$ | unit only |
| SDKs | different bit orders and units | one canonical reading | prevents order and half-turn errors |

: The integrations, with and without the scale. {#tbl-comparison35}

**Verdict.** Two integrations add something the library does not have: heralded calibration, which separates temperature and
readout, and ZNE of the filtered reading with the cost rule. The learning ones open up use without improving accuracy, which
is what Chapter 20 had already measured. The rest are translation: readings in m-qg and a single qubit order, which is little
but prevents real errors, such as pytket's half-turns. No figure comes from hardware. The proposals have not been sent to
any project yet.

## In code {#sec-code35}

```python
# pip install "qang[mitiq]"   (or qang[experiments], qang[sklearn], qang[integrations], ...)
from qang.integrations import mitiq as qm

executor = qm.qg_executor(sampler, weight=1)             # circuit -> mean filtered qg_Z
value = qm.execute_with_filter_zne(circuit, sampler, weight=1, scale_factors=(1, 3, 5))

from qang.integrations.qiskit_experiments import HeraldedReadout
exp = HeraldedReadout([0], backend=backend, frequency=5e9)
results = exp.run().block_for_results()                  # e01, e10, p_excited, m_eq, T_eff

from qang.integrations.sklearn import WeightQNNClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
GridSearchCV(WeightQNNClassifier(gamma=0.15), {"qang": [True, False]}, cv=3).fit(X, y)
```

## Summary {#sec-summary35}

- qang 0.13.0 has `qang.integrations`, with twelve libraries, one extra for each and tests that skip themselves.
- mitiq: the filter with ZNE lowers the error from 55.9 to 1.1 m-qg under T1 and dephasing; post-selection already existed.
- qiskit-experiments: heralded calibration gives unbiased $e_{01}$, $p$ and $T_{\text{eff}}$, where the standard one sees the
  qubit as cold.
- QuTiP, Stim, Qiskit Dynamics and the SDKs get readings in m-qg and the filter, and the four SDKs share the same qubit order.
- scikit-learn, JAX and PyTorch let weight networks train like any other model, without an accuracy gain.
- Three environment conflicts are documented: Qiskit Dynamics with Qiskit 2, PennyLane with JAX ≥ 0.9 and Braket with
  cloudpickle.

## Bibliographic notes {.unnumbered}

mitiq is @larose2022; QuTiP, @johansson2012; Stim, @gidney2021, and PyMatching, @higgott2022. qiskit-experiments is
@kanazawa2023, and Qiskit Dynamics, @puzzuoli2023, on top of Qiskit [@javadiabhari2024]. scikit-learn is @pedregosa2011; JAX,
@jax2018; PyTorch, @paszke2019, and PennyLane, @bergholm2018. Qibo is @efthymiou2021; pytket, @sivarajah2020; Amazon Braket,
@braket; Cirq, @cirq, and CUDA-Q, @kim2023. The symmetry verification mitiq already does is that of @bonetmonroig2018 and
@mcardle2019, and zero-noise extrapolation, @temme2017. The code is in the repository [@qangrepo]; the definition of the qang
unit is in @monteverde2026.
